6. Use hydrologic soil groups A–D

Part 1

Water that plants can use

Field capacity, wilting point and the forms of soil water

Important definitions

Key idea

Plants can use the water held between field capacity and the permanent wilting point.

  • Field capacity: the maximum water content a soil can hold before gravity drainage starts
  • Permanent wilting point: water is held so tightly that plants cannot take it up. Plants stop transpiring and wilt
  • Soil moisture deficit: the water needed to raise the moisture content back to field capacity

Read the figure

Left to right: saturated soil, soil at field capacity, and soil at the wilting point during drought.

Hygroscopic, capillary and gravitational water

Key idea

Soil water comes in three forms; only capillary water is the main supply for plants.

Hygroscopic water

Very thin films bound to particles by adhesion in the micropores. Cannot be removed under normal conditions; not available to roots, but microbes can use it.

Capillary water

Remains after gravitational water drains, held in mesopores and micropores by surface tension. The main water available to plants.

Gravitational water

Drains downward through the macropores. Not available to plants because it drains so quickly.

Soil moisture through the seasons

Key idea

Soil moisture is mainly a balance of precipitation and evaporation, with soil type and vegetation changing the rates.

The annual cycle (Pacific Northwest style)

  • Autumn: rainfall recharge
  • Winter: maximum soil storage
  • Spring: some evaporation loss
  • Summer: most depleted

Read the right figure

After rain the soil is saturated; a few days of drainage brings it to field capacity (about half the pores full); weeks of drought take it to the wilting point.

Plant response to soil water content

Key idea

Plants grow best in the capillary water range, between the wilting point and field capacity.

Read the graph

  • Below the wilting point (about −15 bars): hygroscopic water only, no growth
  • Between wilting point and field capacity (about −0.1 bar): plant available water (PAW)
  • Above field capacity: gravity water drains away; near saturation roots lack air and productivity falls

The critical value (0.4–0.6 PAW) marks where plants start to feel stress.

Plant available water vs. texture

Key idea

Loams hold the most plant available water: sands hold too little, and clays hold water too tightly.

Read the left graph

Both field capacity and wilting point rise from sand to clay. The gap between them, the PAW, is widest in the middle textures (silt loams and loams).

Read the right graph

At every suction, clay holds more water than loam, and loam more than sand.

Water film thickness and moisture tension

Key idea

As the water film around particles gets thicker, moisture tension decreases, and water becomes easier for plants to take.

Read the graph

Both axes are logarithmic. Thin films (hygroscopic water) are held at very high tension; the wilting point is about 15 bars; field capacity is about 0.1 bar.

Below field capacity tension is low and the water is gravitational.

Managing soil moisture for crops

Key idea

Knowing soil moisture lets farmers keep crops in the optimal range and conserve water.

Soil moisture behavior matters for crop management and best agricultural practices.

With good ET estimates, precipitation forecasts and soil moisture data, farmers can manage and monitor crop growth, especially where drought is a problem.

Read the chart

Irrigate when moisture falls to the management allowable depletion line, before it reaches the stress zone and the wilting point.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q1 A soil holds 0.32 m³/m³ at field capacity and 0.12 m³/m³ at the wilting point. How much plant available water is in the top 0.5 m?

PAW = 0.32 − 0.12 = 0.20 m³/m³; × 0.5 m = 0.10 m (100 mm).

Q2 Why is gravitational water not available to plants?

It drains quickly downward through the macropores, so it leaves the root zone before plants can use it.

Q3 Why do loams hold more plant available water than sands or clays?

Sands hold little water at field capacity; clays hold a lot but much of it is held too tightly (high wilting point). Loams have the widest gap between the two.

Part 2

How water moves in soil

Tension gradients, hydraulic conductivity and infiltration capacity

Direction of water movement

Key idea

Soil water redistributes along gradients of soil water tension, not soil water content.

Read the figure

Sand (θ = 8%, −250 mb), loam (θ = 20%, −400 mb) and clay (θ = 25%, −600 mb) touch. Water moves from sand → loam → clay: toward the highest suction, even though the clay already has the most water.

Water always moves from lower tension (wetter, in energy terms) to higher tension (drier, in energy terms).

Hydraulic conductivity: the ability to transmit water

Unconsolidated depositsK (m/d)RocksK (m/d)
Gravel100 – 1000Basalt0.0003 – 3
Coarse sand20 – 100Granite0.0003 – 0.03
Medium sand5 – 20Limestone10−5 – 1
Fine sand1 – 5Sandstone10−3 – 1
Silt0.01 – 1Shale5×10−8 – 5×10−6
Clay10−8 – 0.01
Key idea

Hydraulic conductivity (K), or permeability, is the ability to transmit water, in m/day.

Higher porosity and larger, connected pores generally mean higher K, so soils usually transmit water faster than rocks.

Read the table

K spans more than 10 orders of magnitude: from 1000 m/d in gravel to 10−8 m/d in clay.

Fractured rocks such as basalt and limestone have wide ranges because water moves through fractures.

Infiltration capacity: the sponge example

Key idea

Once a sponge is completely saturated, it reaches its infiltration capacity, and excess water becomes runoff.

Factors controlling infiltration

  1. Soil properties
  2. Vegetation and soil fauna
  3. Land use and management
  4. Antecedent moisture conditions
  5. Precipitation
  6. Water viscosity and quality
  7. Topography

The next part walks through these factors.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q4 A wet clay layer sits under a drier sand. Water moves from the sand into the clay. How is that possible?

Water moves along tension gradients, not water-content gradients. The clay holds its water at higher suction, so it pulls water from the sand.

Q5 From the table, roughly how many times faster does water move through coarse sand than through silt?

Coarse sand is 20–100 m/d; silt is 0.01–1 m/d. That is roughly 100 to 10,000 times faster.

Part 3

What controls infiltration

Soil properties, hydrologic soil groups, topography, vegetation and land use

Soil texture

  1. Texture
  2. Structure
  3. Density
  4. Porosity
  5. Color
Key idea

Texture is the mix of sand, silt and clay: the coarse vs. fine balance of a soil.

  • Sand: 2.00 – 0.05 mm, no plasticity
  • Silt: 0.05 – 0.002 mm, little or no plasticity
  • Clay: < 0.002 mm, high plasticity

Use the triangle

A soil with 30% clay, 10% silt, 60% sand plots in the sandy clay loam class.

Soil structure

  1. Texture
  2. Structure
  3. Density
  4. Porosity
  5. Color
Key idea

Structure is how particles group into aggregates. It shapes the pores that water flows through.

Shapes

Granular, blocky, prismatic and platy. Platy structure stacks horizontally and slows downward flow.

Five size classes of aggregates

  1. Very fine or very thin
  2. Fine or thin
  3. Medium
  4. Coarse or thick
  5. Very coarse or very thick

Soil density

  1. Texture
  2. Structure

  4. Porosity
  5. Color

Quartzite (rock)2.65
Key idea

Soil density reflects the mineral and organic makeup of a soil. We usually report bulk density: how compact the particles are.

Higher bulk density means less pore space and slower infiltration.

Urban soils (lawns, fill, athletic fields) are often as dense as glacial till.

Soil color

  1. Texture
  2. Structure
  3. Density
  4. Porosity
  5. Color
Key idea

Soil color depends on organic matter, drainage, mineral composition and degree of oxidation.

Scientists use color to indirectly estimate other important soil properties.

  • Dark colors: usually more organic matter
  • Red and yellow: oxidized iron in well-drained soil
  • Gray or mottled: poor drainage, often waterlogged

Infiltration capacity of sand and clay

Key idea

Coarse soils keep a high infiltration capacity; fine soils drop to a low one.

  • Gravel and coarse sands: > 0.8 in/hr
  • Sandy loams: 0.4 – 0.8 in/hr
  • Loams: 0.2 – 0.4 in/hr
  • Silty clay loams and clays: < 0.2 in/hr

Terms

Infiltration: entry of water into soil by gravity and tension forces. Infiltration rate: quantity per unit time. Infiltration capacity: the rate when water ponds on the surface. Cumulative infiltration: total depth infiltrated over time.

Hydrologic soil groups

Soil groupCharacteristicsMin. infiltration capacity (mm/hr)
ASandy, deep and well drained8 – 12
BSandy loams, moderately deep and well drained4 – 8
CClay loam, shallow sandy loams, low permeability1 – 4
DHeavy clay, water-logged soils over an impermeable layer0 – 1
Key idea

Hydrologic soil groups A–D rank soils from highest (A) to lowest (D) infiltration capacity.

Developed in the 1950s by the USDA, originally for sizing road culverts on farms.

Group D soils produce the most runoff.

Soil profile and topography

Key idea

Topography strongly influences soil development, and so infiltration.

  • Hillsides: soils tend to be shallow, because of erosion
  • Hilltops: deep but lighter in color, because of downward leaching
  • Valleys: deeper, darker, with more horizons, from deposition of eroded material, accumulation of leached material, and more water collecting in low areas

Read the figure

Down the slope, profiles shift from well drained to very poorly drained.

Vegetation and soil fauna

Key idea

Vegetation and soil animals have direct control on water entering the soil.

Role of vegetation

  • Protects soil from packing by raindrops; prevents erosion and detachment of sediment
  • Provides organic matter that binds particles and supports soil fauna

Soil fauna (e.g., earthworms)

  • Raise the hydraulic conductivity of soil
  • Increase porosity; improve soil structure and fertility

Land use and management

Key idea

Compaction and impervious surfaces cut infiltration; good management can restore it.

Agricultural practices

  • Row crops vs. grassland
  • Soil compaction by machines and animals raises density and shrinks pores
  • Surface roughness from tillage

Urbanization

  • More impermeable surfaces → sheet flow
  • A need for more porous pavement

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q6 Use the texture triangle: what is the texture class of a soil with 30% clay, 10% silt and 60% sand?

Sandy clay loam.

Q7 A new subdivision is built on HSG B soil, and the lawns end up with bulk density 1.8 g/cm³. What happens to infiltration and runoff?

Compaction reduces pore space, so infiltration falls and the soil behaves more like group C or D, producing more runoff.

Q8 From the porosity table, which soil has the largest gap between porosity and field capacity, and what does that mean?

Loamy sand (0.35). Much of its pore space drains by gravity, so it drains quickly and holds little water after rain.

Part 4

Measuring soil water

Infiltrometers, oven drying, tensiometers, resistance blocks and neutron probes

Infiltrometers and rainfall simulators

  1. Infiltrometer
  2. Gravimetric
  3. Tensiometer
  4. Resistance blocks
  5. Neutron probe
Key idea

Infiltration is measured by applying water to the ground and recording how much soaks in over time.

Infiltrometer

Water is supplied at a constant or falling head, and the operator records how much infiltrates from the inner ring into the soil over a time period.

Rainfall simulator

Sprays artificial rain at a known intensity over a plot, so infiltration and runoff can be measured under storm-like conditions.

Gravimetric method

  1. Infiltrometer
  2. Gravimetric
  3. Tensiometer
  4. Resistance blocks
  5. Neutron probe
Key idea

Weigh a field sample, dry it in an oven, and weigh it again. The mass lost is the water.

  1. Weigh the field sample
  2. Dry it in the oven
  3. Reweigh the sample

Then compute G or θ as in Lecture 5d.

Pros

Can be done in a simple lab. It is the standard other methods are calibrated against.

Cons

Problems with sample disturbance and evaporation, and it destroys the sample.

Tensiometer

  1. Infiltrometer
  2. Gravimetric
  3. Tensiometer
  4. Resistance blocks
  5. Neutron probe
Key idea

A tensiometer measures soil water tension through a porous ceramic cup, read by a gauge or transducer.

Parts (top to bottom)

  • Sensor head and pressure sensor (gauge)
  • Water-filled tube
  • Porous cup in contact with the soil

How it works

As the soil dries, it pulls water out through the cup, creating suction in the tube. The gauge reads that tension directly, which is what roots “feel”.

Electrical resistance blocks

  1. Infiltrometer
  2. Gravimetric
  3. Tensiometer
  4. Resistance blocks
  5. Neutron probe
Key idea

Resistance blocks measure electrical conductivity, which is proportional to moisture content.

A porous block (often gypsum) with two wires is buried in the soil and takes up water to match the soil.

The more water, the lower the resistance, and the higher the electrical conductivity.

Cons

Not good in wet soil for a long time: gypsum blocks slowly dissolve.

Neutron probes

  1. Infiltrometer
  2. Gravimetric
  3. Tensiometer
  4. Resistance blocks
  5. Neutron probe
Key idea

A radioactive source emits high-speed neutrons; the number of slow neutrons returning measures soil water.

Fast neutrons are slowed by collisions with hydrogen atoms. The return of slow neutrons to the detector is a function of the soil’s hydrogen content, which is proportional to water content.

The probe is lowered down an access tube to read moisture at different depths.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q9 Which method measures soil water tension directly, and which measures water content by mass?

Tensiometer measures tension. The gravimetric (oven-drying) method measures water content by mass.

Q10 Why does a resistance block show lower resistance in wetter soil?

Water with dissolved ions conducts electricity. More water in the block means more conductive paths, so resistance falls.

Part 5

A preview of the Horton infiltration model

An equation for how infiltration capacity falls during a storm

The Horton infiltration model

Key idea

Horton: infiltration capacity starts high (f0) and decays exponentially to a constant fc.

fp = fc + (f0 − fc) e−kt

  • fp: infiltration capacity
  • fc: equilibrium infiltration capacity
  • f0: initial (maximum) infiltration rate
  • k: decay constant depending on soil type
  • t: time from the beginning of rain

Assumptions

  1. Freely drained soil
  2. Constant rainfall intensity
  3. Water ponded on the surface

k depends on soil type

Key idea

The larger the k, the faster infiltration capacity drops to its constant rate.

Read the graph

All three curves start at the same f0 and end at the same fc. With k = 9 the curve reaches fc quickly; with k = 2 it declines slowly.

k is soil-type dependent, and is found by fitting the equation to infiltrometer data.

More on this model in later lectures.

Infiltration and runoff on a hyetograph

Key idea

Rainfall above the Horton curve becomes runoff; rainfall below it infiltrates.

Read the figure

The bars are a hyetograph (rainfall intensity over time). The falling curve is fp.

Early in the storm the curve is above most bars, so nearly all rain soaks in. Later, as fp falls, the bar tops (shaded) exceed it and run off.

This is Horton overland flow, the first runoff mechanism in Lecture 5f.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q11 For a soil with f0 = 60 mm/hr, fc = 10 mm/hr and k = 2 /hr, what is fp after 1 hour?

fp = 10 + (60 − 10) e−2 = 10 + 50 × 0.135 ≈ 16.8 mm/hr.

Q12 Rain falls at a steady 20 mm/hr on that soil. Roughly when does runoff begin?

When fp drops to 20: 10 + 50e−2t = 20 → e−2t = 0.2 → t ≈ 0.8 hr (about 48 minutes).
